pairs.en: Drives convection currents in the mantle, which move tectonic plates.
Circular loops of hot rising and cool sinking rock in the asthenosphere; the force that moves tectonic plates.
At subduction zones, descending plates melt from extreme heat and pressure, forming magma.

pairs.es: less dense magma rises through the mantle
pairs.en: Magma is less dense than solid rock, so it rises buoyantly toward the surface.
Oceanic (basaltic) crust is denser than continental crust, causing it to subduct at convergent boundaries.
Curved chain of volcanic islands formed when one oceanic plate subducts beneath another.
Mountains formed by magma rising through the crust at convergent boundaries.
Formed when two continental plates collide and compress, forcing rock upward (e.g., the Himalayas).
Underwater mountain range at a divergent boundary where magma rises and forms new oceanic crust.
Long, narrow ocean-floor depression where one plate subducts beneath another at a convergent boundary.
Where a denser oceanic plate sinks beneath another plate into the mantle.
New oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges as plates separate and magma fills the gap.
A valley formed when a continental plate pulls apart; may eventually become a new ocean.
Tectonic plates are constantly in motion due to convection currents in the mantle.
A fixed pool of magma beneath a plate that creates volcanoes at the surface, independent of plate boundaries (e.g., Hawaii).
Where two oceanic plates meet; forms trenches, island arc volcanoes (convergent) or mid-ocean ridges (divergent).
Where oceanic plate subducts beneath continental plate; forms deep-sea trenches and volcanic mountains.
Where two continental plates collide; forms large mountain ranges.
Two plates move toward each other and collide.
Two plates move apart; magma rises to form new crust.
Two plates slide horizontally past each other; no crust created or destroyed.
Continental plate pulls apart, forming a rift valley that may fill with water to become a new sea.
Steep, layered volcano at subduction zones; violent explosive eruptions.
Broad, flat volcano from fast-flowing lava; found at hotspots; calm eruptions (e.g., Hawaii).
The underground point where an earthquake originates.
Point on Earth's surface directly above the focus; strongest shaking occurs here.
Instrument that records seismic waves; 3 stations needed to locate an epicenter.
Fastest seismic waves; travel through solids and liquids; arrive at stations first.
Slower seismic waves; cannot travel through liquids; stopped by Earth's liquid outer core.
Focus near the surface; causes the most severe damage.
Focus deep underground; less surface damage than a shallow quake of equal energy.
Caused by compression; hanging wall moves up.
Caused by tension; hanging wall moves down.
Caused by shearing; rocks slide horizontally past each other (e.g., San Andreas Fault).
